I forgot to summarize the issue. 
The above change will not fix the issue because the issue is *not* that the `urllib.parse.urlparse()` "does not decode the escaped %25 character back to %." as noted above. 
The issue is that the CPython library `urllib` does not not parse the url string to generate a host string that is enclosed with "[" character. Therefore, when we use urllib3 to manage ConnectionPool objects, the `urllib3.util.url._normalize_host()` which is called from the constructor of `ConnectionPool()` objects does not detect the host address as IPV6 address and this is where things go wrong.
Clearly, it would seem urllib's `urlparse()` api  is not compatible with urllib3. So since we use urllib3 to manage connection objects, one obvious choice is to use urllib3's `parse_url()` method instead.  It would make things uniform. It would not remove the "[" characters from the host part and seems this api is spec compatible as well.
This is what I have proposed in the above PR I sent out. As a consumer of this library, we have done our part to analyze and suggest a possible solution. Rest, we leave to the maintainer of this library.

There are a number of different behaviors that can happen when using `requests` with a URL containing IPv6 address with a zone ID, depending on the first two characters of the zone ID. For example:
- %4, %20, %afsd: works.
- %30, %531, %6a: triggers the bug from #6808 where the first two characters get mistakenly interpreted together with the % as a percent-encoded unreserved character. Depending on the main part of the IP address this can result in an incorrect but valid address with no zone ID (e.g. fe80::1%30 becomes the valid IP address fe80::10) or result in an invalid IP address that will throw an exception (at a `urlparse` invocation within `prepare_cookies`).
- %eth0: gets passed to `getaddrinfo` with a percent-encoded zone separator, i.e. %25eth0. `getaddrinfo` understands "25eth0" as the zone ID and raises a `gaierror` (Name or service not known). This is the bug present in the current issue, #6735.

[This script](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27717474/getaddrinfo_trace.py), which overrides `socket.getaddrinfo` to see what it ends up receiving after a top-level call to `requests.get`, can be used to reproduce these observations (without actually running any requests or calls to the real getaddrinfo); run it as `python getaddrinfo_trace.py 'http://[fe80::1%531]/foo'`.

The relevant RFCs are:
- [RFC 4007](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc4007/): specifies the format of IPv6 addresses with a zone identifier, e.g. `fe80::1%1`
- [RFC 6874](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc6874/) (obsolete): specifies how IPv6 addresses with zone identifiers should be represented in URLs, e.g. `http://[fe80::1%251]/foo`. I believe `requests` is intended to adhere to this spec.
- [RFC 9844](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9844/): explicitly retracts 6874, so there is no longer a specification for how to include zone identifiers in URLs.

Detailed pipeline of the bugs, which mostly happen in `PreparedRequest.prepare_url`:
- the URL is parsed using `urllib3`'s `parse_url`. Both the RFC-6874-compliant form `http://[fe80::1%251]/foo` and the relaxed form `http://[fe80::1%1]/foo` are accepted, and the function `_normalize_host` ensures that the parsed host contains a bare % in both cases.

  - a zone starting with two characters which are hex digits which are not ASCII code for an unreserved character: not affected, the output of `requote_uri` is `http://[fe80::1%20]/foo`.
  - a zone starting with two characters which are hex digits which are ASCII code for an unreserved character, e.g. %531: the % sign and following digits are unquoted to the corresponding character, which yields the URL `http://[fe80::1S1]/foo`.

The above change will not fix the issue because the issue is *not* that the `urllib.parse.urlparse()` "does not decode the escaped %25 character back to %." as noted above. 
The issue is that the CPython library `urllib` does not not parse the url string to generate a host string that is enclosed with "[" character. Therefore, when we use urllib3 to manage ConnectionPool objects, the `urllib3.util.url._normalize_host()` which is called from the constructor of `ConnectionPool()` objects does not detect the host address as IPV6 address and this is where things go wrong.
Clearly, it would seem urllib's `urlparse()` api  is not compatible with urllib3. So since we use urllib3 to manage connection objects, one obvious choice is to use urllib3's `parse_url()` method instead.  It would make things uniform. It would not remove the "[" characters from the host part and seems this api is spec compatible as well.
This is what I have proposed in the above PR I sent out. As a consumer of this library, we have done our part to analyze and suggest a possible solution. Rest, we leave to the maintainer of this library.

This issue occurs only when TLS is enabled on both the client and server sides.

When a `requests` client sends a large `PUT` request and receives an **HTTP 307 redirect**, the server may close the connection early before the payload is fully transmitted. This happens because the server issuing the redirect does not need to process the request body, so it terminates the connection as soon as it sends the redirect response. However, `requests` does not handle this scenario gracefully and raises the following SSL error:
```
urllib3.exceptions.SSLError: EOF occurred in violation of protocol (_ssl.c:2426)
```
## Expected Result

If an HTTP 307 redirect is received before the payload is fully transmitted, `requests` should handle the redirect properly **without complaining on the previous early-closed connection**. The client should not fail simply because the server closed the connection early.

## Actual Result

`requests` fails with `SSLEOFError` instead of retrying the request to the redirected location.
This issue does not occur with small payloads (maybe because they are typically sent in a single transmission chunk and completes before the server closes it?)

```python

requests.put("https://localhost:5000/", data="A" * 10_000_000, verify="/path/to/openssl/certs/ca.crt")
